source.title: Training Faster by Separating Modes of Variation in Batch-Normalized Models

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares batch normalization with mixture normalization and reports classification test accuracy or error, including training and test curves. This is a different intervention from the listed claim versions, but its results bear on test generalization.
record.gate_note: No listed version directly tests random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected models, optimizer generalization, large-batch effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Results cited from prior work are not rows. GAN FID results concern generation rather than the claim's classification generalization.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates mixture normalization against batch normalization, which tests none of V1–V8. Section 2.1 cites prior large-batch generalization findings relevant to V5 but supplies no batch-size comparison of held-out performance. RMSprop and Nesterov experiments use different training recipes and do not isolate V4. Temporal test-error stability does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly captures the authors' claim: MN accelerates training in gradient-update counts and usually improves held-out classification performance. Its exception statement needs correcting: Table 2 also shows CIFAR CNN MN-3 slightly below BN-3 on CIFAR-10, besides the explicitly acknowledged Inception-V3 CIFAR-100 exception. Reported acceleration is not directly a wall-clock speedup because MN increases per-update computation.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates mixture normalization against batch normalization; it does not implement the listed versions' interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with dataset, learning rate, weight decay, mixture-normalization layer placement, mixture components and EM iterations, architecture, optimizer, and learning-rate decay policy.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing selected BN layers with MN usually improves reported maximum test accuracy or best test error. Exceptions include CIFAR CNN MN-3 on CIFAR-10 (77.33% versus 77.35%) and Inception-V3 MN-1 on CIFAR-100 (70.43% versus 71.30%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixture normalization often improves held-out classification performance over batch normalization in the tested CIFAR recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.2 reports smoother test-error trajectories and suggests a connection to flat minima, without measuring magnitude-scaled weight perturbations or correlating sharpness with generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixture normalization reduces temporal fluctuations in test error in the reported CIFAR CNN experiments.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The paper reports test-accuracy tables and training/test curves but does not provide uncertainty estimates for most table entries. It says one standard deviation is shown for the curves; plotted values are not transcribed here. The reported final test-performance comparisons do not directly quantify the training-test gap.
record.rows_left_out: GAN FID measurements were left out because they concern generative image quality rather than classification test generalization. Other accuracy entries in Tables 2 and 4 were omitted where paired BN/MN settings were redundant with the selected conditions; figure-only training/test curves were not transcribed as numerical rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization under comparable tuning budgets and recipes.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epochs and adapted training recipes; discussed only through prior work.
Dropout addition, removal, strength, and interactions with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with training–test gaps, and ranking against other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded numerical performance values agree with the supplied text, but they measure the study's normalization method rather than V1–V8. Tables 2 and 4 report maxima attained within the epoch budgets, not necessarily accuracy at the final epoch. Shaded standard deviations describe variation across neighboring epochs, not uncertainty across independent runs. No additional result bearing on a listed version requires a missing-row entry.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
Held-out performance comparisons among adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers.
Large-batch versus small-batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
